scope: arithmetic and design conclusion only; no flash, no COM, no RF, no firmware change
problem: the gate hardware microsecond clock is 32 bits and wraps at 4294967295 us, which is 71.583 minutes. main.c stops the whole runtime on a backwards clock. Gate D requires a 60 minute soak with both contexts live, so a session that crossed the wrap would stop in the middle of the measurement with no fault of its own
conclusion: the soak fits. The clock counts from boot, so a 60 minute soak started from a fresh boot ends at 60 minutes with 11.58 minutes of margin before the wrap, and SESSION_LIMIT_US at 65 minutes is itself below the wrap. No firmware change is required and none is made

what_was_deliberately_not_done.widening_or_wrapping_the_clock: rejected. The backwards-clock stop is a deliberate safety property of the V17..V25 lineage: a clock that went backwards means no timestamp in the evidence can be trusted, and every ACK deadline measurement rests on those timestamps. Teaching the runtime to continue across a wrap would trade a real safety stop for the convenience of a longer soak, and it would have to be proven on hardware to be worth anything
what_was_deliberately_not_done.reasoning: the constraint is not a defect to be engineered away here. It is an operating envelope, and the honest response is to declare it and enforce it where the soak is planned

enforcement_belongs_to_the_host.where: the Gate D guard, not the firmware
enforcement_belongs_to_the_host.check: read time_us from STATUS before starting the soak and refuse to start if time_us plus the soak duration plus a margin would exceed the wrap. The host owns the soak plan and is the only party that knows how long the soak is going to be
enforcement_belongs_to_the_host.effect: a soak is either started from a fresh boot with provable room, or it is not started at all. It is never started into a wrap and then stopped halfway
